jobs.title: Why do you want this new job
jobs.description: No matter which side of the table youâve sat during interviews, youâve probably heard this question: âWhy do you want this new job?â In the recent past, Iâve interviewed a few candidates and heard the following answers so far: Iâm not learning much on the current job after itâs been 2-4 years. Iâm looking for something that offers better work-life balance. Iâm not really looking for a job. The recruiters got in touch and I thought Iâd discuss. Iâm looking for more challenging work. All of the above are valid answers. I think thereâs another perfectly valid answer that candidates seldom mention probably due to the gravity of the interview room situation. Iâve interviewed over a hundred candidates across different companies and am yet to find anyone that mentions: I am not happy with my current salary and benefits compared to my skills Back to topic of answers. So, when someone answers that they are not learning new things on the job, obviously, youâd be curios to know why and how they have tried to change things. Unfortunately, most candidates simply mention that they are doing repeat work and thereâs not much to learn doing the same thing over and over again. This is where I start feeling a little uneasy. However, I understand that itâs a true statement. If youâre in a similar situation, hereâs some suggestion: read books, and write code based on what youâve read. Then, you can tell a much convincing story that, Iâve forced myself to learn new things and hereâs some proof, but I really want to apply the newly learned skills outside the scope of the âhello worldâ skills. About work-life balance, I totally hear you. And if your current job doesnât suit what you need out of your life, itâs a perfectly valid reason to look for new opportunities. However, make sure youâre able to clearly set the expectation with your potential employer about what work-life balance means for you. For example, if you canât work over 40 hours a week, or must work from home one-two days a week, itâs best to discuss this even before an interview starts to ensure youâre a good match with the employer. If you showed up at in interview just because a recruiter got in touch, Iâd say introspect first. Itâs possible that on our subconcious mind you have expectations that the potential of the new job offers you something that you donât get at the current job. So, instead of a passive asnwer that the you simply acted based on the recruiterâs invite, itâs much convincing to see if you can lay down one or two things that you expect from the new job that you donât get at the current job. About looking for more challenge, it sounds like a cliche unless you can share examples of work that is of challenging to you. Applying data-centric ML methods such as hard-example mining, resampling/reweighting and curriculum or balance adjustments to lift model performance. jobs.description: Are you a theoretical mathematics expert eager to shape the future of AI? Large-scale language models are rapidly advancing, and their ability to handle rigorous proof-based reasoning depends on high-quality mathematical training data. With your advanced expertise, tomorrow’s AI can better understand abstraction, logic, measure theory, homotopy, and the deep structures of modern mathematics. That training data begins with you - your insight will help power the next generation of AI. We’re looking for specialists with deep foundations in pure mathematics who can engage with advanced topics across probability theory, measure theory, real and functional analysis, optimization, abstract algebra, and category theory. Coupled with this deep foundation, we need each expert to have a normalized fluency in Lean 4, the proof assistant and programming language. On a typical day, you will construct and evaluate complex proofs, substantiate the mathematical reasoning for correctness and rigor while identifying subtle conceptual or logical failures, and translate this material to successfully build in .lean syntax. You will also collaborate with our team to refine prompts, evaluation frameworks, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, enhancing the overall quality of our operations. Candidates fluent in Lean 4 with an in-progress or freshly earned PhD or current PostDoc experience in pure mathematics are ideal. A strong command of core areas is required, and applicants should be comfortable with topics such as Markov’s and Chebyshev’s inequalities, Hoeffding bounds, convergence theorems, the Carathéodory extension theorem, the Riesz representation theorem, Banach–Alaoglu, Lax–Milgram, stochastic approximation, Van Kampen’s theorem, the Yoneda embedding, and representability in cohomology. Clear, metacognitive communication (explicitly articulating reasoning and proof strategies) is essential. Ready to turn your Lean 4 fluidity and pure math expertise into the reasoning backbone of tomorrow’s AI? Apply today and help teach the model that will support researchers, scientists, and engineers around the world. jobs.title: CircleCI: Senior Software Engineer
jobs.description: Headquarters: Remote, Ontario, Canada About CircleCI Engineering CI/CD has been solved. Now it's being reinvented. AI agents don't just run pipelines. They write code, trigger builds, interpret failures, and propose fixes. The interfaces that developers use to understand and trust that work don't exist yet. We're building them. At CircleCI, our guiding principles aren't posters on a wall. We learn fast: we run experiments, accept failure, and scale what works. We think like the customer: every decision connects back to the developer sitting in front of a failing build at 2 am. We own the outcome: not just our slice of it, but the whole thing. If that's how you already work, you'll fit here. Team-Agnostic Placement We don't hire for a team. We hire for CircleCI. Where you land depends on where your strengths create the most leverage, and we figure that out together. You might own the CI pipeline experience, deploy and release tooling, notification infrastructure, monetization flows, AI agent surfaces, or the foundational web platform. The through line across all of it is the same: full-stack ownership, a high bar for craft, and work that directly shapes how tens of thousands of developers experience CircleCI every day. What You'll Do Build AI-natively. AI is how we work. It's not a productivity layer on top of engineering, but the default starting point for how problems get approached and solved. Set technical direction. You define the approach others build from. When the problem is complex or the answer isn't obvious, you're the person who leads the design discussion, writes the ADR, and makes the call. Invent new interfaces. Software delivery is being reinvented. Pipelines run autonomously, generate fixes, and surface results that need human judgment. The tools developers use to understand, trust, and act on that work don't exist yet. You'll define what they look like and establish the patterns the team builds on. Own the full stack. Build features end-to-end in Go, React, and TypeScript. You don't hand off at a layer boundary. You own the outcome. Obsess over craft. Reliability and responsiveness are design concerns, not afterthoughts. Care about how the interface holds up when stakes are high and hold your team to that same standard. Champion observability. Use Honeycomb, Datadog, and Rollbar to understand and improve your systems. Operational data drives stability, not just incident response. Close gaps and fix the conditions that created them. You'll notice gaps and close them. When a gap reflects something broken in how the team works, you fix that too. What You'll Bring AI-native engineering practices. You use AI tools daily and can speak to what you've built, where they changed your approach, and where they fall short. A track record of shipping. You've built something real and put it in front of users. 5+ years of production full-stack experience, with latency, responsiveness, and reliability treated as design concerns, not afterthoughts
